title: The Spirit's Work and Sorrow Turned to Joy
summary: Jesus warns the disciples that they will be expelled from synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God. He tells them it is for their good that he goes away, because then he will send the Advocate, who will convict the world about sin, righteousness, and judgment and guide the disciples into all truth. Using the picture of a woman in childbirth, he promises that their grief will turn to joy, and he ends by telling them that though they will have trouble in the world, he has overcome the world.
story: This is the last part of Jesus' teaching in the farewell discourse before his prayer in chapter 17. Chapter 15 ended with the world's hatred; chapter 16 makes the threat concrete and then answers it. The disciples are full of sorrow (16:6), confused by talk of a little while (16:16-19), and about to scatter (16:32). Jesus doesn't hide what is coming. He tells them in advance so that they will not fall away (16:1), and he gives them three things to hold: the Spirit's coming, the joy of seeing him again after the resurrection, and the Father's own love. The chapter's final word, “I have overcome the world” (16:33), is spoken on the eve of what looks like total defeat.
historical:
Jesus foresees that the disciples will be put out of the synagogues and that some who kill them will think they are serving God (16:2). The New Testament records exactly this in the first generation. Saul of Tarsus, before his conversion, persecuted the church out of zeal for God (Acts 8:1-3; Galatians 1:13-14; Philippians 3:6), and Stephen and James were killed (Acts 7; 12:2). In these conflicts both sides were Jews: the apostles were Jews arguing with fellow Jews about whether Jesus was Israel's Messiah.

There is a bitter irony in later history. When the church gained power in the Roman Empire and in medieval Europe, Christians persecuted Jews, and at times killed them, believing they were serving God. Jesus' warning about religious violence in God's name applies to his own followers as much as to anyone. A faithful reading of 16:2 must name that reversal and refuse any use of the text to excuse contempt for Jewish people.
cultural:
Being expelled from the synagogue (see the note on 9:22) meant losing one's place in the Jewish community: its worship, its fellowship, and often family and business ties. For Jewish followers of Jesus in the first century, this was a heavy cost. The word Jesus uses for offering a service to God (latreia) was used of the worship offered at the temple, which shows how sincerely the persecutors could believe they were right.

The picture of a woman in labor was common in the prophets for the sudden, painful arrival of God's new age (Isaiah 26:17-19; 66:7-14; Micah 4:9-10). In the ancient world childbirth was dangerous and often fatal for mother and child, so the image held real fear as well as hope. Jesus uses it to say that the disciples' grief over his death will be like labor pains: real anguish, but anguish that gives way to new life.
literary: The chapter alternates between warning and promise. It begins with persecution (16:1-4), turns to the Spirit (16:5-15), then to the puzzle of the little while (16:16-24), and finally to plain speech and the coming scattering (16:25-33). The phrase “a little while” appears seven times in 16:16-19, emphasizing how close both the parting and the reunion are. Jesus says he has been speaking in figures of speech (paroimia, the same word as in 10:6) but that an hour is coming when he will speak plainly. The disciples claim that hour has arrived (16:29-30), but Jesus' reply shows that their confident belief is about to be tested. The discourse ends not with the disciples' strength but with his: “take courage; I have overcome the world!”

outline.t: A little while: grief turned to joy
Plain speech, scattering, and victory over the world

doctrines.note: The Spirit will convict the world in regard to sin, righteousness, and judgment (16:8-11), and will guide the disciples into all truth, speaking what he hears and glorifying Jesus (16:13-14). The Spirit's work is to point to Christ, not to himself, and to bring to light what the world will not see.

“Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine,” and the Spirit takes what is Christ's and makes it known (16:15). The three persons share one work: the Father gives, the Son possesses and reveals, the Spirit discloses. The Son's sending of the Spirit shows the Spirit's close relation to both Father and Son.

After the resurrection the disciples will ask the Father directly in Jesus' name, “For the Father Himself loves you” (16:27). Prayer in Jesus' name is not persuading a reluctant Father through a mediator but approaching a Father who already loves them.

words.note: Elegchō, to convict, expose, or prove wrong. It can mean to bring something to light, to prove guilt, or to rebuke. Here the Spirit acts almost like a prosecutor, reversing the world's verdict on Jesus: the world judged him a sinner, but the Spirit shows that the world's sin is unbelief, that Jesus was righteous as his return to the Father proves, and that the real one condemned is the prince of this world.

Paraklētos, the Advocate. In 16:7 Jesus says it is to their benefit that he goes, because only then will the Advocate come. The legal sense of the word is prominent in this chapter, where the Spirit takes the role of an advocate in the trial between Jesus and the world.

Hodēgeō, to guide or lead the way. The Spirit “will guide you into all truth” (16:13). The word pictures leading someone along a road, and it echoes Jesus' claim to be the way (14:6). The Spirit leads the disciples deeper into the truth that Jesus is.

Nikaō, to conquer or overcome, related to nikē, victory. “I have overcome the world” (16:33) uses the perfect tense, speaking of the victory as already won, before the cross. The same word is used in 1 John 5:4-5 and throughout Revelation for the victory of Christ and those who belong to him.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus' confidence in the face of death: he speaks of his going as his return to the Father who sent him (16:28), and of victory before the battle. It also shows his care. He tells the disciples in advance what will happen so they will not be shaken, and he promises that the Spirit will continue his work. The image of labor pains looks ahead to the resurrection: the grief of Good Friday will give way to Easter joy, which no one can take away. John's readers know that Jesus will indeed be left alone by his disciples, and that he was not alone, because the Father was with him (16:32).

hard.q: Does the promise that the Spirit will guide “into all truth” mean God gives new revelation today?
hard.a:
Christians agree that the Spirit's guidance in 16:13 was given first to the apostles, whose witness became the New Testament, and many read the verse as God's promise behind the writing of Scripture. They differ on how it applies beyond the apostles. Many Protestants hold that the Spirit's work now is to illuminate Scripture, giving understanding of what God has already revealed, and that no new revelation adds to it. The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that the Spirit guides the church as a whole, preserving and unfolding apostolic truth through its tradition and teaching authority. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians affirm that the Spirit still speaks through gifts such as prophecy, while most insist that such words are tested by Scripture and never equal to it.

All these views agree that the Spirit's guidance glorifies Christ (16:14) and does not contradict what he has said, since the Spirit speaks only what he hears. Claims of new truth that lead away from Jesus fail the test Jesus himself sets. How the Spirit's ongoing guidance relates to Scripture and to the church is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree.

questions: Jesus says it is better for the disciples that he goes away. When has something that felt like loss turned out to be for your good?
The persecutors in 16:2 believed they were serving God. How can sincere religious conviction become cruelty, and how might you guard against it?
Jesus promises trouble in the world and peace in him. Which of those do you tend to forget?
